hints: Start from the definition of pressure as force per unit area and identify which force the liquid exerts on the base.
Write the mass of the liquid using density and the volume of the liquid column in terms of $A$ and $h$.
Combine the weight of the liquid with the pressure definition and cancel the area $A$ to leave $p$ in terms of $\rho$, $g$ and $h$.
teacher_walkthrough: Pressure is defined as normal force per unit area: $$p = \frac{F}{A}$$
The force on the base due to the liquid is the weight of the liquid: $$F = W = mg$$ so $$p = \frac{mg}{A}$$
Density is defined as mass per unit volume: $$\rho = \frac{m}{V}$$ so $$m = \rho V$$
The liquid forms a column of area $A$ and height $h$: $$V = Ah$$ so $$m = \rho A h$$
Substitute into the pressure expression: $$p = \frac{\rho A h g}{A}$$
The area $A$ cancels to give: $$p = \rho g h$$
walkthrough: State $m = \rho V$ with $V = Ah$ leading toward $p = \rho gh$.
Use weight over area $mg/A$ to complete $p = \rho gh$.
common_pitfalls: Using mass instead of weight for $F$, giving $p = \rho h$ or $p = m/A$ with no $g$.
Stating $V = Ah$ without linking $m = \rho V$ and $F = mg$, so the derivation has missing steps.
Failing to show cancellation of $A$, leaving the proof incomplete.

hints: Consider what else is pushing down on the top surface of the liquid in addition to the liquid itself.
teacher_walkthrough: Total pressure at depth includes pressure transmitted from above the liquid surface.
The beaker is in air, so atmospheric pressure acts on the free surface of the liquid and is transmitted through the liquid to the base.
The expression $p = \rho g h$ accounts only for the liquid column, so total pressure is $p_{total} = p_{atm} + \rho g h$.
walkthrough: Atmospheric or air pressure also acts on the surface and on the base.
common_pitfalls: Stating that air pressure acts only at the surface and not recognising it adds to pressure at the base.
Confusing gauge pressure due to liquid with absolute total pressure.

hints: Write total pressure as intercept plus $\rho g x$ and identify what the gradient of the pressure against $x$ graph represents.
Read a large $\Delta p$ and corresponding $\Delta x$ from Fig. 4.2, converting the axis units of $10^4$ Pa and cm to Pa and m.
teacher_walkthrough: Total pressure varies with depth $x$ as: $$p_{total} = p_{atm} + \rho g x$$ This is a straight line with intercept $p_{atm}$ and gradient $\rho g$.
Select two widely separated points, for example $x = 0$ where $p = 9.60 \times 10^4$ Pa and $x = 8.0$ cm where $p = 9.66 \times 10^4$ Pa.
Change in pressure: $$\Delta p = (9.66 - 9.60) \times 10^4$$ $$\Delta p = 0.06 \times 10^4 = 600 \text{ Pa}$$
Change in depth in SI units: $$\Delta x = 8.0 \text{ cm} = 8.0 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m} = 0.080 \text{ m}$$
Set gradient equal to $\rho g$: $$\rho g = 7500$$ $$\rho = \frac{7500}{9.81}$$ $$\rho \approx 7.6 \times 10^2 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$$
common_pitfalls: Forgetting to multiply the y-axis readings by $10^4$ or forgetting to convert $x$ from cm to m, giving density out by powers of 10.
Using a single point $p/x$ instead of $\Delta p/\Delta x$, which incorrectly includes the atmospheric intercept.

hints: Recognise that the initial 0.53 N reading with the cylinder just touching the liquid is the weight, and that full immersion adds an upthrust equal to the weight of displaced liquid.
Calculate the displaced volume from $V = A L$ and set up $U = \rho V g$ using the density from (c).
teacher_walkthrough: When the base is level with the surface no liquid is displaced, so tension equals weight: $$W = 0.53 \text{ N}$$

When fully immersed with top level with surface, displaced volume equals cylinder volume: $$V = A L$$ $$V = (3.7 \times 10^{-4}) \times (4.0 \times 10^{-2})$$ $$V = 14.8 \times 10^{-6} = 1.48 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m}^3$$

Upthrust equals weight of displaced liquid: $$U = \rho V g$$ Using $\rho \approx 7.6 \times 10^2 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$: $$U = (7.6 \times 10^2) \times (1.48 \times 10^{-5}) \times 9.81$$ $$U \approx 0.11 \text{ N}$$
For stationary equilibrium, tension plus upthrust balance weight: $$T_{new} + U = W$$ $$T_{new} = 0.53 - 0.11$$ $$T_{new} \approx 0.42 \text{ N}$$
walkthrough: Calculate upthrust as $\rho Vg = \rho \times 3.7 \times 10^{-4} \times 4.0 \times 10^{-2}$ giving about $0.11 \, \mathrm{N}$.
common_pitfalls: Adding upthrust to weight instead of subtracting, predicting tension increases on immersion.
Using length or area alone as displaced volume instead of $V = A \times L$, or mixing up cm and m conversions.
